name: The Unmourned (the Gray Zone Sending)
description:
No one knows exactly when 'The Unmourned (the Gray Zone Sending)' first appeared. The oldest confirmed recording dates to 2189, but the song's structure — a slow processional built on a pentatonic modal frame with Andean huayno rhythmic inflections and Yoruba call-and-response phrasing — suggests folk evolution over decades, not single authorship. It is attributed by convention to the Feroza Yards Singers, a loose assembly of the Gray Zone Block 3 dock families. The lyrics address the dead directly, acknowledging that no official record will mark their passing, that no corporate memorial will be filed, that the city will not slow — and declaring, simply, that those present remember. The final verse is always sung without accompaniment, in unison, regardless of how many or how few people are present.

The song has no fixed key, no fixed tempo, and no authoritative text — it is relearned orally in each community that adopts it, absorbing local variation and dialect. Recordings circulate on physical chips because neural feed versions, which would fix the song in one interpretation, are considered by the Gray Zone communities to miss the point. The song is meant to be sung imperfectly, together, in a cold room or a damp tunnel or an alley, because that is where the Gray Zone people die and where the Gray Zone people grieve.
creator: Feroza Yards Singers (attributed)
genre: the Gray Zone folk, funeral processional, oral tradition
audience: the Gray Zone communities, dock workers, anyone burying someone outside the official corporate memorial system, labor organizers, underground medics
cultural_impact: The song functions as GLMZ's most significant counter-memorial tradition — a direct rejection of the corporate grief-management industry, which offers tiered funeral packages denominated in Φ and stores the deceased in data archives accessible only to paying family subscribers. Singing 'The Unmourned' is an assertion that memory belongs to community, not to Vantablack Media's memorial services division. It has spread upward into Tier 2 and even some Tier 3 communities, particularly among those who have lost someone to industrial accident, corporate negligence, or enforcement action. Its presence at a funeral is now sometimes read as a political statement.
known_fans: Tier 2 workers with the Gray Zone origins
story_hooks: A Vantablack Media subsidiary has quietly begun filing trademark claims on specific melodic phrases associated with the song, with the long-term goal of controlling its use — someone needs to find and document every variant before they can be suppressed.
A Tier 4 executive attends a the Gray Zone funeral incognito and hears the song for the first time, and it breaks something open in them that their expensive grief counselor never could.

An oral historian from outside GLMZ arrives to document the song's variants and discovers that one version, sung only in a single the Gray Zone block, contains encoded information — names, dates, and cause of death — for people whose records were officially deleted.
